phonemes.desc: The first syllable, [so]: an unaspirated sibilant plus a mid back rounded vowel, carrying the phrase-initial prominence of the Korean reading.

The second syllable, [ɕin]: an alveolo-palatal fricative — the sharper Korean 시, tongue raised higher than in English sh — plus a dental nasal. It is the Sino-Korean word 신 神, 'deity, spirit', the second element of the name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SOH-sheen' — two syllables with a light stress forward; the sh-sound is the crisp Korean 시, slightly sharper than English 'sh'. In shamanic usage the name denotes a spirit who reveals hidden matters and carries messages between realms.

kin.label: Sino-Korean 神
kin.form: sin (신), 'deity, spirit' — the second element of the name, borrowed from Middle Chinese (modern Mandarin shén); the same cognate morpheme Korean shares with Chinese and Japanese religious vocabulary

kin.label: Korean ritual term
kin.form: jeollyeongsin (전령신), 'messenger spirits' — the attested class name of the courier spirits of the gut, to which Sosin belongs (Lee Jung Young, Korean Shamanistic Rituals, 1981)

kin.label: Comparative
kin.form: the spirit-messengers of Chinese wu mediumship and the courier spirits of Siberian and Tungus shamanism — a regional type rather than a uniquely Korean invention (Walraven, Songs of the Shaman, 1994)

pronunciation.note: Sosin is Tier 2: the restoration adds only the capital of a proper name, and the normalized form is plain ASCII. The Hangul reading gives the 시 a palatal onset [ɕ] that ASCII cannot show, but the tier system keys on preserved diacritics and distinctive letters, of which there are none.

domains.title: Sosin, the Revealer of Things
domains.subtitle: messenger spirit who discloses hidden causes and conveys prayers
domains.lead: Sosin (소신) is a messenger and revealer spirit of Korean shamanic (musok) cosmology — one of the jeollyeong, the courier spirits who open the road between the human village and the spirit bureaucracy, carry petitions upward, and bring back the diagnosis of what ails a household: which spirit is offended, what taboo was broken, what offering will mend it.

cards.name: Revealer of Things
cards.desc: Sosin uncovers the hidden causes of misfortune and illness.

cards.desc: Sosin helps the shaman read signs and diagnose spiritual problems.

cards.name: Ritual Intercessor

mythology.lead: Sosin has no scripture, no temple, and no canonical myth cycle. The figure lives inside the gut — the Korean shamanic rite — in the invocations, divinations, and petitions that ethnographers have recorded from mudang over the past century. The ritual narratives below cluster around the messenger-revealer role; the attestation is thin and regional, and the tradition itself holds that such spirits are known only through the rite.

myths.title: The Government of Heaven
myths.text: Korean shamanic cosmology, as the gut manuals and ethnographic records describe, models the spirit world on the old Korean state: a celestial bureaucracy of generals, ministers, and magistrates presided over by figures such as Cheonha Daejanggun, the Generalissimo of All-under-Heaven, with the mountain gods, household gods, and ancestors arranged in ranks below (Lee Jung Young, Korean Shamanistic Rituals; Walraven, Songs of the Shaman). Petitions do not ascend by themselves. The jeollyeong — the messenger spirits, of which Sosin is named as one — are the couriers of this government: they open the road at the rite's beginning, announce the household's business, and carry the answers back down. No classical text tells a story of Sosin the way the Kojiki tells of Ninigi; the evidence is the practice itself, recorded village by village. The figure's meaning is structural: in a cosmos run like a court, revelation is a bureaucratic act, and the messenger is the hinge on which both prayer and diagnosis turn.

myths.title: Opening the Road
myths.text: Every gut begins by making a way. The shaman sets out the divination flags and the offering table, drums the spirits toward the house, and invokes the road-opening messengers so that the petitions of the living can reach their recipients. Ethnographers of the twentieth century — among them Boudewijn Walraven, working from recorded mudang performances, and Laurel Kendall, working in and around Seoul — describe how the early sequences of a chaesu-gut, the rite to restore fortune, are addressed precisely to these courier spirits. Sosin belongs to this opening phase: the revealer who first names what is wrong. The ritual logic is exact — before the offended god can be appeased, someone must say which god, and the saying itself is the messenger's work. In this way the humblest stratum of the rite, its postal service, is also its epistemology: knowledge of the invisible arrives the way a sealed letter does, handed on from spirit to spirit until a human mouth can open it.

myths.title: Reading the Cause of Illness
myths.text: When illness has no visible cause, Korean households have long turned to the mudang. In the rite's divinatory passages the shaman interrogates the spirits on the client's behalf: has a household god been neglected, was a taboo broken at a birth, a death, a move, does an ancestor want something? The messenger-revealer spirit is the one addressed to disclose the answer. Laurel Kendall's ethnography of Seoul-area shamans (Shamans, Housewives, and Other Restless Spirits, 1985) records how the diagnosis is negotiated in performance — the shaman's body the instrument, the spirits' answers arriving through song, movement, and the casting of divination implements. The sources never make Sosin the author of a doctrine; the tradition grants the figure a humbler dignity, as the one who makes hidden causes speakable. The interpretive point is the one Korean shamanism keeps returning to: misfortune is a message, and someone must carry it before it can be answered.

myths.title: The Petition Ascends
myths.text: A gut is also a delivery. The household's petitions — for a child's health, for a business, for peace with a dead relative — are composed in the rite, set with offerings on the altar, and then, in the tradition's own idiom, sent up. The messenger spirits carry them from the household's humble gods through the mountain and village powers to the celestial offices, and return bearing the answer: do this, offer that, mend this relationship. Lee Jung Young's classic account (1981) describes the gut as structured along exactly these postal lines, and Walraven's transcriptions of shamanic song show the couriers addressed by name and title. It is tempting to call Sosin a minor figure, since no epic survives; but rites of this kind are performed to this day across the peninsula. The myth, in the end, is the mailbox itself — the faith that what is spoken in the village is heard above.

etymology.derivation: The name is probably composed of 소 (so, "small" or an element in words of announcing/revealing) and 신 (sin, "spirit, deity"). Its meaning in shamanic usage emphasises disclosure and communication rather than hierarchy.

nameVariations.note: Standard romanisation of the Hangul name.
Honorific form used in vernacular address, with the Korean suffix of respect -nim (님); the earlier '-sama' form was a Japanese borrowing and has been corrected.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Sosin, the Hangul form is 소신. Hangul ‘소신’; no single canonical Hanja is fixed for this shamanic figure. The ASCII form sosin is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Sosin is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Sosin sits at the meeting point of several centuries of Korean religious politics. Confucian literati classed the mudang's messengers among the 'heterodox spirits' their order condemned; Buddhist establishments, more accommodating, absorbed the spirit hierarchy as mundane deities below the Buddha; and the Protestant churches that loom large in modern Korea inherited much of the old Confucian distrust of the rite. Japanese colonial authorities moved against shamanic practice in the 1930s and 1940s, and post-war governments stigmatised it as superstition before folklorists rebuilt its scholarly standing. Related rites have since received formal honour — the Jeju Chilmeoridang gut was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2009. Comparatively, the messenger-revealer type is regional rather than uniquely Korean: Chinese spirit-medium traditions and the courier spirits of Siberian shamanism present the same courier of a celestial bureaucracy, and Sosin is best read as the Korean member of that type (Walraven 1994; Lee 1981).
lore.culturalLegacy: Sosin is not a household name in the way that Yongwang or Samshin are, but it remains important within shamanic practice and the academic study of Korean religion. The figure appears in ritual manuals, recordings of gut performances, and ethnographic studies of mudang; the famous twentieth-century shaman Kim Keum-hwa and others carried the gut to national and international stages, turning village ritual into recognised performance art. Sosin also stands in the background of Korea's enormous contemporary fortune-telling culture of saju and jeom — the commercial grandchildren of the village mudang's diagnosis. And it interests modern readers concerned with divination, intuition, and the hidden dimensions of experience. As Korean shamanism gains international scholarly attention, figures like Sosin help illustrate the complexity and sophistication of the tradition: a religion whose postal service is also its theology.
lore.extendedMeditation: Sosin is the patron of an unfashionable idea: that truth needs a courier. The modern world imagines that information travels by itself, weightless and instant; the Korean gut remembers that it never does. Between the village's grief and heaven's answer stands a being whose whole office is the passage — someone who opens the road, states the petition plainly, and brings the reply back in terms a household can act on. Every translator, every advocate, every doctor who reframes a frightening diagnosis is doing Sosin's old work. There is also a quiet lesson in the figure's obscurity: the tradition gave no epic to its messengers because their perfection is invisibility. They are judged, as postal workers are, by whether anything arrives. To restore the capital S is to grant that office a name, and to admit that some of the most consequential figures in any cosmology are the ones who only carry.

lore.archaeology: No inscription, stele, or excavated shrine names Sosin; the figure's 'archaeology' is the archaeology of the gut itself. The material witnesses are the ritual paraphernalia preserved in Korean collections — the National Folk Museum of Korea in Seoul holds shamanic costumes, divination flags, bells, blades, and mirrors from twentieth-century performances — and the documented regional cycles of gut performance: the Jeju yeongdeunggut (inscribed by UNESCO in 2009), the chilseong-gut and jeseok-gut traditions recorded across the peninsula. Film and audio recordings of mudang made by scholars from the 1970s through the 1990s now function as the primary 'texts' for spirits of this class. Older strata are indirect: the Confucian and Buddhist polemics against 'exorcists and spirit-mediums,' reaching back well over a millennium, attest the tradition's antiquity even as they condemn it.
